trajectory_summary: The call opens cold and degrades steadily once the credit-score question surfaces a contradiction the customer had already flagged in the ad ('no charge'). The rep never resolves the free-vs-qualify tension, drifts into unprompted product/spec talk under pressure, and the customer disengages twice before the rep releases him. This is a clean disqualification/decline, not a fragile booking.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep captured a usable bill range early but never referenced it again, including at the final save attempt (04:36) where citing the customer's own number would have been the strongest available leverage.

bill_document_audit.reasoning: The call ended in a decline before the rep reached the bill-collection stage of the script; only a verbal average was captured, no request for the actual bill document was made.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: Objection inversion on the 'free vs. credit check' contradiction
primary_coaching_focus.quote: It's just to qualify. Like, you need a 70 670 to qualify for it.
primary_coaching_focus.why: This is the exact moment the call turns — the customer's very next line is 'I'm not interested.' The rep had a clean objection_inversion opportunity (flip the free-ad framing into 'what's not free is your current bill') and instead gave a literal, defensive answer that let suspicion compound for the rest of the call.

key_moments.quote: It's just to qualify. Like, you need a 70 670 to qualify for it.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is a textbook objection_inversion trigger — customer questions why a 'free' program needs credit qualification — but the rep answers literally instead of flipping it (e.g., reframing the qualifier as protecting the customer's own bill savings). The customer's very next line escalates to 'I'm not interested,' suggesting the literal answer accelerated disengagement rather than defusing it.

key_moments.quote: drawn up some kind of prospects, man. I've been in sales my whole life.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer self-identifies as sales-experienced and labels the approach a lead-gen tactic. This is a trust/legitimacy crisis moment, not a standard cost objection, and calling for honest specificity about the program mechanics rather than continued generic reassurance.

key_moments.quote: well, like I said Sorry, buddy. Because we're not I'm not a salesman. I just have to set up appointments and help build design.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is the rep's attempt at a trust-building move — disclaiming salesman status to differentiate from the pushy tactic the customer is accusing him of. It is a legitimate escape-hatch instinct (correctly scoped: 'I just have to set up appointments'), but it's poorly executed and undercut by the immediately preceding and following lines where the rep re-engages in program/product explanation.

key_moments.quote: We have the we're partnered with Tesla, and we use the all black panels, and they're very pretty. They're very sturdy. They're, like, literally bulletproof, and they they work great.
key_moments.stewart_read: Unprompted panel-spec description volunteered while the customer is actively expressing distrust — this is exactly the scope-creep anti-pattern (rep explaining panel technology unprompted) and it does nothing to address the actual trust objection on the table.
